1:
Why so solemn an opening is needed they explain from what is coming. Gill says the apostle, about to discourse of predestination and of the rejection of the Jewish nation, prefaced it with strong assurances of his attachment to that people, lest he be thought to speak from prejudice. Henry says such a profession was requisite to take off the odium he might incur by proving their rejection, and adds that it is wisdom to mollify truths which sound harshly, since a nail dipped in oil drives the better. Wesley says the same in a line. Barnes reads the chapter as opening a new train of argument designed to meet objections against the positions already defended. Adam Clarke, following Taylor, frames the whole as continuing the proof that God's mercy is free to all who believe, against the merit of works or of any law. Calvin states the difficulty most fully: the Jews, for whom Christ was appointed according to the covenant of the law, not only rejected him but for the most part hated him, from which either there was no truth in the divine promise or the Jesus whom Paul preached was not the Lord's anointed; and this twofold knot the apostle unties in what follows.

The form of the asseveration Robertson counts precisely: a triple oath, so strongly is he stirred, a positive affirmation in Christ, a negative one in denying that he lies, and an appeal to conscience as co-witness in the Holy Spirit. Ellicott paraphrases the first clause as meaning that from the bottom of his soul, in the most sacred part of his being, as a Christian man united to Christ, he makes this asseveration; and he takes conscience here very much in the modern sense, the introspective faculty which sits in judgment upon actions and assigns their moral quality, overshadowed by the Spirit and therefore incapable of self-deception. Theodoret says he proves that what he was about to say should be free from all falsehood, since he calls the grace of the Spirit to witness with his conscience. Chrysostom, preaching on it, says he had seemed the day before to speak exorbitant things of Paul's love toward Christ, yet what is heard today is as far above those things as those were above our own.

The two words for the grief Gill distinguishes carefully, the one signifying a grief which has brought heaviness on the spirits and the other such pain as a woman in travail feels; and the trouble was internal, in the heart, not lying merely in outward show. Robertson notes that the word for consuming grief and the adjective for unceasing are both rare, each occurring in the New Testament only here and once in the letters to Timothy, from which he draws some small argument for the Pauline authorship of the Pastoral Epistles. Barnes insists the word rendered continual must be taken in a popular sense: not that the apostle was literally always pressed down by this sorrow, but that whenever he thought on the subject he had great grief.

Calvin and Theodoret both notice that the sentence is deliberately broken off. Calvin says he dexterously manages so to cut short his sentence as not yet to express what he was going to say, since it was not yet seasonable openly to mention the destruction of the Jewish nation, and thus intimates a greater measure of sorrow, imperfect sentences being for the most part full of pathos. Theodoret makes the same observation, that the composition of the sentence is incomplete, since it should have been added that the sorrow was caused by the infidelity of the Jews; through caution he omits the words and teaches in the sequel that he so meant. Wesley draws a different lesson from the same clause, that a high degree of spiritual sorrow and of spiritual joy may consist together.
3:
The first question is what the verb allows. Gill reports a reading he then refuses, that the wish belongs to the apostle's unregenerate state, when as a persecutor he wished to be for ever separated from Christ and to have nothing to do with him; but he answers that no one would appeal to Christ in so solemn a manner, and take an oath upon it, for the truth of an enmity which everybody already knew. Barnes lays out three objections to the same past reading: that the design is to state present attachment and present willingness to suffer, that the grammar gives not I did wish but I could desire, and that the apostle never in fact wished to be devoted to destruction by the Messiah, since he never doubted that in persecuting he was defending the hopes of his nation against an impostor. Robertson settles it on the form itself, an idiomatic imperfect meaning I was on the point of wishing; the present would be wrong to say, and the constructions with the particle would put the wish either out of reach or too remote, so the apostle is shut up to the imperfect indicative. Ellicott renders it I could have wished, the wish relating to what was really impossible, a nobly generous impulse at which some weak minds have been shocked and out of which others have made sentimental capital.

What the curse itself means Theodoret explains from usage. The word has two significations, for what is consecrated to God bears that name and so does what is separated from him, and he shows the second from the closing words of the letter to the Corinthians and the first from the devoting of Jericho; here the apostle uses the second, and says not that he could desire but that he could pray to be separated from Christ, provided his kindred in the flesh, being united to him, should reap salvation. Calvin reaches the same sense and presses it: another word added proves that eternal and not merely temporal death is meant, since to be separated from Christ is to be excluded from the hope of salvation, and it was proof of most ardent love that he did not hesitate to wish for himself the condemnation he saw impending over others. Ellicott asks whether the intensity of the expression does not help us realise one aspect of the atonement, in him who was made a curse for us, the Greek word there being different though nearly equivalent.

Whether the wish was lawful is answered by the manner of it. Calvin meets the doubt by fixing the boundary of love, that it proceeds as far as conscience permits: if we love in God and not without his authority our love can never be too much, and the apostle, seeing his own nation endued with so many divine benefits, loved the gifts in them and them on account of the gifts, and counted it a great evil that such gifts should perish. He adds that such ardour sees nothing but the object in view, so that election was not weighed against the wish but passed by while he was wholly intent on their salvation. Wesley says human words cannot fully describe the motions of souls that are full of God; in how high a sense he wished it none can tell, but he did not then consider himself at all, and the thing could not be, yet the wish was pious and solid, with a tacit condition if it were right and possible. Clarke, paraphrasing with Taylor, reduces the sacrifice to exclusion from the visible Church and sets it beside Moses offering to be blotted out rather than see the people destroyed, remarking that few passages have puzzled critics more, since read literally no man in his right mind could wish himself lost to save another.
4:
Gill begins with the name itself, borne as descendants of Jacob and accounted very honourable, and says it gave the apostle concern that such a people should be cut off. Clarke presses further: the name implied a royal nation, princes of the most high God, and the adoption took place when God made the covenant with them at Horeb. Robertson notes that the relative means the very ones who, inasmuch as they, that the covenants are plural because renewed again and again, and that the term for the giving of the law occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Theodoret takes each privilege with its proof: the name was imposed by God himself on their forefather and transmitted as an heirloom, the adoption is secured by the word calling Israel his son and firstborn, the glory belongs to them as having been illustrious through miracles, and the covenants include not the old only but the new which he had promised to make with the house of Israel, though this they themselves were not willing to accept.

On one item the readings divide. Barnes takes the glory as the symbol of the divine presence that attended them from Egypt and rested over the ark, Ellicott and Robertson name it the Shechinah, Clarke adding that this was peculiar to the Jews. Wesley denies it: the apostle speaks not of the ark or any corporeal thing, but God himself is the glory of his people, so that adoption and glory are relative terms, God being the Father of Israel and Israel the people of God. Wesley also orders the list, counting six prerogatives whose first pair respect the Father, the second Christ, the third the Holy Spirit, and observing that the covenant was given long before the law and is plural because so often repeated, having two dispositions, one promising and the other exhibiting the promise. Ellicott insists the covenants are not the two tables of stone but the several compacts made with Abraham and his descendants, while Clarke reports that some take the singular for the plural and the decalogue as meant.

Calvin explains why the catalogue is here. The relative pronoun stands for a causal adverb, so the reason for the anguish is plainly given: it was because they were Israelites, and the Lord had by a kind of privilege so raised them that they were separated from the common order of men. These titles of dignity were testimonies of love, since we speak so favourably only of those we love; and though by ingratitude they had rendered themselves unworthy of esteem, the apostle continued justly to respect them, that we might learn that the ungodly cannot so contaminate the good endowments of God but that they always deserve praise, while those who abuse them acquire only the greater guilt.

The last privilege raises the largest question. Ellicott states the controversy: Trinitarian and English interpreters as a rule take the closing words of the Messiah, while others put a full stop after came and make the remainder a doxology to God. Both ways are possible, and the question is which is more natural, prepossessions being set aside, since we are not to read meaning into Scripture but to elicit meaning from it. He finds the word order somewhat in favour of the first, since a formal doxology would more naturally begin with the ascription of blessing, and the context also, the break becoming rather abrupt otherwise. Robertson agrees that this is the natural punctuation and that a full stop before the doxology is abrupt and awkward. Barnes calls the appellation one belonging only to the true God and notes there are no various readings of consequence. Clarke says the apostle here distinctly points out the twofold nature of our Lord, and Wesley that the original words imply the self-existent Being who was and is and is to come.
6:
Clarke states the objection in a Jew's mouth: is not God bound to continue this people as his peculiar Church, and if they are levelled with the Gentiles has he not failed of his promise to Abraham? Wesley says they imagined the word of God must fail if all their nation were not saved. Gill answers that the apostle speaks partly to relieve his own mind and partly to prevent the mistake, since whether the word means the prophecies, now about to be accomplished, or the gospel, which had had its effect on the chosen among that people, it had not fallen. Henry says we are not to ascribe inefficacy to any word of God, for nothing he has spoken can fall to the ground, and the rejection of the Jews by the gospel did not invalidate the promise made to the patriarchs. Calvin reads the turn as a recovery of composure: carried by his wish into an excess of feeling, the apostle returns to his office as a teacher and restrains immoderate grief, anticipating the inference that the covenant had failed and showing that God's favour continued still.

The answer is a distinction inside the name. Robertson translates flatly, that not all out of the literal nation are the true Israel, and observes that this startling paradox is no new idea nor a clever dodge, since he had already shown that those of faith are Abraham's sons. Barnes says not all the descendants of Jacob have the true spirit of Israelites, and that the promise will not fail though he does not affirm that the whole nation is to be destroyed. Ellicott notes a mixture of two constructions in the opening words, and says the promise was given to Israel but did not mean roundly all who could claim descent from Jacob. Wesley reduces it to a rule: God accepts all believers and them only, which is no way contrary to his word.

The proof is taken from the household itself. Calvin says the hidden election of God overrules the outward calling and yet is not inconsistent with it but tends to its confirmation, and argues from the strongest case: if any natural progeny ought not to have fallen away it was those who obtained the privilege first, so that when one of Abraham's own sons was separated as the seed while he was yet alive and the promise new, much more might the same befall his distant posterity. Clarke presses the same from Ishmael, circumcised before Isaac was born, in whom Abraham desired the promise fulfilled and God might have fulfilled it had he pleased. Barnes says the choice implied election at the very commencement of the nation's history, so that as God then rejected part of the natural descendants he might do so still. Ellicott takes the words to mean that in Isaac Abraham should have posterity called his, thus excluding the seed of Hagar, and Gill notes how highly the Jews valued being the natural seed.

What made Isaac the seed was the promise. Ellicott says these are not merely promised children but children born through the miraculous agency of the promise, which is regarded as possessed of creative power. Wesley says Isaac was conceived by the power of the promise, not of nature. Gill calls the birth a produce not of nature but of divine grace, typical of the regeneration of the elect. Cyril of Jerusalem takes Abraham as the standing example: God promised the old man a child when his body was dead in regard to offspring and no hope was left, and he heeded not his own weakness but the power of him who promised. Calvin notes the quotation follows the Hebrew rather than the Greek, Robertson that two verses are combined, and Clarke that the apostle gives only a hint of each passage, expecting the whole to be read and judged there.
10:
A second example is brought because the first could be evaded. Clarke supplies the evasion: a Jew might say Ishmael was rejected not by God's sovereign will but as the son of the bondwoman, and so unworthy. Calvin answers that the case is now beyond such a plea, for these were of the same mother and even twins, yet one was rejected and the other chosen; and he notes that the sentence is again broken off before the principal verb. Barnes says the principle settled by the promise is seen again in the family of Isaac, the choice running against nature, the younger preferred and the elder rejected, though by the custom of the times the elder was thought entitled to peculiar honours. Gill marks that the first instance was not the only one, and Robertson notices the idiom by which the mother is said to have a marriage bed of one husband: one father, and twins.

The weight falls on the timing. Barnes lays out what the clause excludes: they had done nothing good or bad, and where that is so there can properly be no moral character, the period of moral agency not having begun, so the distinction lay behind character and was founded in God's purpose. Robertson parses the two genitive absolutes, the children not yet born and neither having practised anything good or worthless, and glosses not of works as not of merit, the source of the selection being God who calls. Calvin says the apostle now ascends higher, to the cause of the difference, nowhere to be found but in the election of God; before he had only hinted how it happened, and now ascribes the whole to an election gratuitous and in no way depending on men, so that nothing higher is to be sought in the salvation of the godly than God's goodness. Wesley says the choice fell before either had done good or evil, showing that their ancestors were not accepted through merit of their own.

Whether the oracle speaks of persons or of nations divides them. Clarke says the word children is not in the text and nations would be proper, and that the personal sense is not true, since Jacob never exercised power over Esau but was rather subject to him and sorely afraid, acknowledging his brother to be his lord. Wesley agrees that the elder served the younger not in person but in his posterity, the Edomites being often brought into subjection. Barnes reads it of the two peoples and their train of temporal and spiritual blessings. Ellicott notes that the words may be rendered the greater shall serve the lesser, the ambiguity standing in the Greek and the Hebrew alike, and that whether age or comparative strength is meant, the nations are intended. Calvin allows the reference to the birthright and yet insists it was the symbol of something greater, since in the flesh Jacob gained little by it, driven from home, unkindly treated in exile, and prostrate in fear at his brother's feet.

The prophet's harder word they handle with care. Barnes says it means no positive hatred but that God preferred the one and withheld from the other the privileges given to Jacob's posterity, love and hatred being commonly used in this comparative sense. Robertson admits the language sounds harsh, notes that the verb does not always carry the full force of what we mean by hate, and says that though the preference and the rejection are not in doubt he hesitates to read into it the intense hatred that afterwards divided the two peoples. Calvin takes the prophet as giving the reason for the primogeniture: the Lord asks what privilege the brother had that he should be preferred, and answers none whatever. Wesley adds that it relates neither to the persons themselves nor to the eternal state of them or their posterity.
14:
Gill notes the form of words the apostle uses when about to introduce an objection. Barnes states the charge often brought against the doctrine, that God does injustice, and says it is strongly repelled and then answered from the older Scriptures and from just views of sovereignty. Ellicott says the apparently arbitrary choice of one and rejection of another seems to imply injustice in him who exercises it, a thought not to be entertained. Robertson observes that the particle expects a negative answer, so that beside God there can be no injustice to any man because of election. Henry sets the frame wider: God is here to be considered not as a governor distributing rewards and punishments by revealed law, but as an owner and benefactor giving such favour as he has determined by his own secret counsel, both visible church membership and effectual grace. Calvin warns that the flesh cannot hear this wisdom without being disturbed by numberless questions and attempting to call God to account; predestination is a labyrinth from which the mind cannot extricate itself, and the more perilous the examination the more boldly curiosity proceeds.

The answer is fetched from Moses. Gill observes that the testimonies come from writings held in great esteem among the Jews, so that full satisfaction might be given. Barnes makes much of the occasion: the words were spoken when God declared he would make all his goodness pass before Moses, so they were given not as proof of stern and inexorable justice but as the very demonstration of his benevolence, and those who call them arbitrary pervert what God offers as kindness. Clarke paraphrases it as a warning against claim: I will make such a display of my perfections as shall convince you that my nature is kind and beneficent, but know that I am a debtor to none of my creatures, and no people, much less a rebellious people, can challenge my blessings as due. Ellicott notes that in the most characteristic period of the older covenant favour was thus promised to Moses and denied to Pharaoh. Calvin adds that the first verb carries the sense of showing favour rather than mercy, following the Hebrew, while the second conveys pity: I will favour whom I choose to favour.

From the testimony an inference is drawn, and it is the apostle's own. Gill insists it is no consequence forced by an adversary, as though men might sit still and do nothing, but the apostle's own conclusion about election. Calvin says election is not to be ascribed to our diligence or striving or efforts but wholly to the counsel of God, who chooses those who neither will nor strive nor even think of such a thing; and he rejects the reasoning that we have some power to strive which merely fails of effect unless assisted. Barnes guards the other side: it does not mean the saved do not choose eternal life or are brought in against their own choice, since the effect of the Spirit is to make a man willing in the day of his power; what is denied is that life is bestowed for any original willingness of his own. Ellicott takes the running for a metaphor from the foot races the apostle may have seen at Corinth, the prize depending not on human will or effort but on grace, and Robertson notes his fondness for the figure. Clarke finds the terms in the history: Abraham willed the blessing for Ishmael, Isaac designed it for his firstborn, Esau ran a-hunting for venison that it might be conveyed to him, and all were disappointed. Wesley sets the will of man against the grace of God and man's running against the divine operation, and extends the declaration to all the spiritual children of Abraham to the end of the world.
17:
Calvin says the apostle comes now to the second part, the rejection of the ungodly, and because there seems something more unreasonable in this he labours to show that God in rejecting whom he wills is not only irreprehensible but wonderful in wisdom and justice; the connecting word reaches back to the question of unrighteousness and might be rendered moreover. Gill says the testimony proves the other branch of predestination and clears it of the charge, and notes that the Scripture saith is a Talmudic formula used when a point is proved from Scripture, equivalent to saying that the merciful God says. Barnes calls it one of the most extraordinary instances of hardness of heart ever known, chosen to show that God may pass by those to whom he will not show mercy and place them where their true character is developed; the haughty king of Egypt proves the mightiest monarchs to be under control. Robertson notes that the earlier verses dealt with a national election while here the apostle deals with individuals, laying down that the grace of God does not necessarily depend on anything but his will.

The verb raised up is variously understood. Barnes says the Greek means properly to excite, rouse or stir up, while the older margin reads made thee stand, that is, sustained thee. Clarke takes it of recovery from the plague of boils, God having restored him to health and respited his deserved destruction to a longer day, that his final overthrow might teach all mankind who is the righteous Judge and avenger of wickedness. Ellicott renders it brought into the world and on to the scene of history, and says the converse is also true, that God uses the wickedness of men to exhibit his power and justice, here by the plagues and the overthrow in the sea. Wesley takes it of making him a great and glorious king, and reads the saying with a condition, that unless he repented this would surely be the consequence; he suggests further that God was resolved to show his power over the river, the insects, the animals, the air and the sun, all worshipped by the Egyptians, and over all their gods at once by the stroke that slew the firstborn. Calvin says he was raised up to this end, that while he obstinately strove to resist the power of God he might, being overcome and subdued, afford proof how invincible that arm is, which no human power can bear, much less resist.

The conclusion is the hard word, and it is carefully bounded. Barnes says hardening here means only what the case specifies, not a positive influence but the leaving of a sinner to his own course where his character is more and more developed, though it implies an act of sovereignty in not putting forth the influence by which he might have been saved. Ellicott observes that the older narrative lays the hardening to the man's own act, which may yet be part of the design of providence, and says the decrees of God include human free will without destroying it, though how we cannot say. Robertson likewise notes that he hardened his own heart, that God also gives men up, and that the verb is a physician's word used by Galen and Hippocrates and found nowhere else in this apostle. Calvin refuses the softening: applied to God in Scripture the word means not permission only, as some washy moderators would have it, but the operation of the wrath of God, and beyond the divine will we are not allowed to proceed. Wesley reads the mercy as shown on God's own terms to them that believe and the hardening as leaving men to the hardness of their own hearts, and Clarke adds that the punishment stands unless prevented by deep repentance.
19:
The objector speaks in his own voice, and they hear his tone. Wesley says the particle still expresses his sour, morose murmuring, and the bare pronoun his surliness and aversion, since he will not deign to name God. Gill calls it the objection of a natural man given up to a reprobate mind, a running upon God upon the thick bosses of his bucklers, rude to the last degree. Calvin says the flesh especially storms when it hears that they who perish were destined to destruction, and that the objectors, not content with defending themselves, make God guilty in their stead and grow indignant at his power, storming because they cannot resist. Robertson notes that the imaginary objector has picked up the admission about the hardening, that still argues a change of condition, and that the verb is perfect, to maintain a stand. Barnes calls it the standing objection against the doctrines of grace, founded on the difficulty of reconciling God's purpose with man's free agency and assuming, unprovably, that a purpose must destroy freedom. Clarke sets it beside the earlier cavil about being judged a sinner though the truth of God abounds through one's lie.

The reply begins by reminding the man what he is. Gill denies that the apostle met an objection he could not answer, and says he silences the insolent creature first by this, that he is man and not God, a creature and not the Creator, and must not expect his Maker to account for his matters. Barnes ranges the impiety under heads: man is a creature, and it is improper he should arraign his Maker; and he is unqualified, a being in the infancy of his existence, to sit in judgment on the Infinite Mind. Clarke turns it on the objector: reflect on thyself, and after abusing the grace of God and transgressing his laws wilt thou cavil at his dispensations? Ellicott says the answer is less a solution of the intellectual difficulty than an appeal to the religious sense to forestall it, since that God's dealings should be questioned at all is a breach of reverence. Robertson notes the emphatic word order and the double compound verb meaning to answer to one's face, and Calvin renders it as entering into a dispute with God.

The figure of the potter carries the rest. Gill observes that a potter has such power over clay he never made but only purchased, much more God who created it. Clarke recalls the prophet's visit to the potter's house and adds that no potter takes pains to make a vessel merely to show he can dash it to pieces. Barnes notes that the prophet's words are preceded by one declaring our righteousnesses to be filthy rags, so that having no claim and no merit they suffer no injustice if favours go elsewhere. Robertson presses the same, that the right claimed is a right over men already sinners. Calvin says the word denotes not strength to do as one wills but a privilege rightly belonging to the maker, no arbitrary power being claimed; as the potter takes nothing from the clay whatever form he gives it, so God takes nothing from man in whatever condition he creates him, and is deprived of part of his honour unless such authority be conceded. Wesley distinguishes two views of the right, God as Proprietor dispensing gifts by rules quite out of our sight, and God as Governor and Judge dealing by rules clearly revealed. Ellicott alone concedes a difficulty: in strict logic the verse confirms rather than refutes the objection, since no one blames earthenware for being badly made, and though the apostle has left that point and is proving another, there is apparently a flaw inseparable from our imperfect conceptions, the two lines of thought running parallel and colliding when drawn together.
22:
The sentence is broken, and both notice it. Ellicott says it is incomplete in the original, the apodosis dropped in the course of the argument, with a second suppression later that would need a clause about the glory reserved; he ascribes the irregularity to the apostle's habit of dictating. Calvin treats the whole as a question with an ellipsis, filled out by asking who can charge him with unrighteousness, since here appears nothing but the most perfect course of justice.

Everything turns on the two participles. Robertson takes the first concessively, although willing, not causally, as the words about much long-suffering show. Wesley reads it the same way: although it was now his will, because of their obstinate unbelief, to show wrath, which presupposes sin, he yet endured with a long-suffering that should have led them to repentance. Ellicott says that while his will was ultimately to execute wrath and display his judicial power, he bore with evildoers and gave them time to repent. Barnes takes the willingness as no objection, since what is right to do is right to purpose. Clarke applies it to Pharaoh and the Egyptians and then to the Jews of the apostle's own day, who had sinned after the same similitude, hardening their hearts and abusing goodness after every display of kindness.

The second participle they handle with more care still. Robertson notes a perfect passive denoting a state of readiness, and observes pointedly that the apostle does not say here that God did it or that they did it, though their responsibility appears elsewhere; the destruction meant is endless perdition, not annihilation. Wesley says they were fitted for it by their own wilful and final impenitence, and Clarke that by obstinate refusal of grace they had fitted themselves, which he calls absolute proof that hardening and punishment alike followed their own refusal. Gill notes that nothing here relates to any act of God before time, all of that having been considered already, so that what is described is his conduct in time toward both sorts. Calvin says the unblamable justice of God shines no less in the perdition of the reprobate than in the salvation of the elect, while no reason is given why this man is chosen and that rejected, God's secret counsel not being meet to be subjected to human judgment.

The other vessel is described by contrast with it. Calvin says the mercy shown the elect is made clearer by the ruin of the rest, since they differ in nothing except that they are delivered from the same gulf, and by no merit of their own but through gratuitous kindness; that mercy appears the more worthy of praise when we see how miserable are all who escape not his wrath. Barnes distinguishes grace as favour to the undeserving from mercy as favour to the miserable. Clarke finds a reason for the timing: the Jews were fitted for destruction long before, but the fittest season came after the believing Gentiles were prepared, since that nation was to supply the first preachers and had to be preserved until the gospel took root. Ellicott says the abstract terms are now explained, the vessels of glory being those meant to accept the Christian teaching, Jew or Gentile, and the vessels of wrath the unbelieving mass of Israel. Gill turns from election to calling as its fruit and evidence, holding that election may be known by calling as a cause by its effect, so that a man satisfied of the one ought to be equally satisfied of the other. Calvin draws two conclusions, that grace is neither so confined to the Jewish people that it cannot flow to other nations nor so tied to them that it reaches all Abraham's children after the flesh. Wesley marks the turn to grace free for all, and Robertson that the proof is now drawn from the older Scriptures.
25:
Henry states why the prophets are brought in: having explained the promise and proved the divine sovereignty, the apostle shows that the rejection of the Jews and the taking in of the Gentiles were foretold in the older Scriptures and must therefore agree with the promise made to the fathers; it clears a truth much to observe how Scripture is fulfilled in it, and the Jews would willingly refer the case to writings committed to themselves. Barnes lists what the quotations establish: that God meant to call a people from the Gentiles, that no promise bound him to save all the Jews, and that he might therefore cut off any of them from their privileges. Clarke says the calling of the Gentiles was no fortuitous thing but a firm purpose largely revealed to the prophets, so that by opposing it the Jews renounced their own prophets and fought against God. Gill notes that it was foretold long before those called were in being, which could have no foundation but God's eternal sovereign pleasure. The spelling of the prophet's name detains two: Clarke complains that no uniformity of orthography has been kept between the Testaments and asks what stranger to our sacred books would take the form used here for Hosea, while Ellicott quotes Lightfoot on whether it should be sounded as two syllables or three.

The real difficulty is that the prophecy was spoken to Israel itself. Calvin states it plainly: no one can deny that the prophet there speaks of the Israelites, whom the Lord, offended at their wickedness, declared should be no longer his people, and to whom he then promised that of those not beloved he would make some beloved; yet the apostle applies to the Gentiles what was expressly spoken to Israel. He reports that those most successful in untying the knot suppose the reasoning to be that what might hinder the Gentiles existed in the Jewish nation too: as God formerly received into favour those he had cast away, so he does now. Barnes reaches the same result: in the prophet the words concern not the calling of the Gentiles but the recalling of rejected Jews, and if God purposed to recall a people he had rejected, the like is not absurd toward another part of mankind. Ellicott says the original concerns the pardon promised the apostate northern kingdom and is here typically applied, since those who had ceased to belong to the chosen people and those who never belonged stood alike. Robertson notes that the prophet refers to the ten tribes while the apostle applies the principle, and that both phrases were names given to the prophet's own children.

On the second citation the readings part. Wesley draws a doctrine from a single word, that one who once was not beloved was consequently not unconditionally elected, and refers the passage to the final restoration of the Jews. Calvin uses the same clause the other way: those are said not to be beloved to whom God declares wrath rather than love, and though they whom he has destined as sons are perpetually his sons, Scripture counts none his children but those whose election is proved by their calling, so we judge of election only as it manifests itself by its own evidences. On the place named, Robertson says it meant Palestine in the original and is applied to scattered Jews and Gentiles everywhere, Wesley that they need not leave their country for Judea, and Gill that it means the very selfsame spot of ground. Ellicott adds a textual doubt, that the Hebrew may mean instead of being called not my people they shall be called sons of the living God, citing Ewald and Hitzig. Clarke reads the two prophecies together, the decrease of the Church by the taking away of the ten tribes being well supplied afterwards by the calling in of the Gentiles.
27:
Calvin says the apostle proceeds now to the second part, with which he was unwilling to begin lest he exasperate their minds, and that the prophet is made to exclaim rather than to speak so that more attention might be excited; the words were meant to keep the Jews from glorying in the flesh, for it was dreadful to hear that of so vast a multitude only a small number should be saved. Gill takes the same word of the prophet's own sorrow, uttered with strong crying and tears, or of his wrestling with God on their behalf, and observes that these testimonies, while proving that some Jews were called, at the same time suggest the casting off of the far greater number. Ellicott refers it to the prophet's impassioned utterance, and Robertson says he cries in anguish over the outlook for Israel but sees hope for the remnant. Barnes notes that the rejection was far harder to establish than the calling of the Gentiles and so needed an explicit passage, and that although the prophet spoke primarily of his own generation the case settled a general principle.

On the word remnant Ellicott insists on the article, the remnant and only the remnant, and adds that the original says shall return to God, the apostle having followed the Greek in putting the consequence of conversion for the conversion itself. Robertson notes the rare noun and the manuscripts divided over it. Calvin explains the application: when the Lord resolved to deliver his people from the captivity, the benefit was purposed for very few of that vast multitude.

The following verse is confessedly hard. Gill reviews four attempts and rejects them all as foreign to the apostle's purpose: an account balanced with a small remainder, the incarnate Word cut off in a short time, the ceremonial law abolished and the moral abridged, and the gospel bringing in a perfect righteousness. Barnes says the quotation keeps the sense but not the words of the Hebrew, that finishing the work means bringing it to an end, and cutting it short means executing it speedily, so that the destruction shall not be delayed. Ellicott renders it a short and summary sentence executed upon the earth, and takes its severity as proof that only a remnant can be saved. Robertson notes the two present participles each compounded with the same preposition, finishing completely and abridging. Clarke calls the terms forensic, from the close of a judicial proceeding in which the Lord has tried and found them guilty. Calvin gives his own sense, that the Lord will so cut short and cut off his people that the residue may seem a consumption, having the vestige of a very great ruin, and Wesley that in rigorous justice he will leave but a small remnant.

The earlier word of the same prophet closes the proof. Ellicott notes that the book was already collected in the form we have it, and that but for this remnant the rejection of Israel would have been utter and complete. Barnes explains the title: the word means hosts and denotes armies organised for war, hence the angels marshalled in military orders and the stars, God being their King and Commander. Calvin observes that the Greek version leaves the title untranslated here as often in this prophet, though elsewhere rendering it of the powers or almighty, and that seed stands for remnant, meaning a small portion reserved for sowing. Clarke draws it out further, that just enough of the righteous were left to be a seed for a future harvest of true believers, so that the godly were not destroyed from the land. Wesley takes the word to denote both the present paucity and the future abundance, and Robertson that the sentence is a condition of the second class, determined as unfulfilled.
30:
Henry says the apostle comes at last to fix the true reason of the reception of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews: there was a difference in the way of their seeking, and therefore that different success, though it was still free grace that made them differ; and he concludes like an orator. Gill takes the question as inviting the objection and answering it, since the calling of many Gentiles and few Jews is chargeable with no unrighteousness but must be referred to sovereign pleasure, and is an instance of grace, all having deserved destruction. Barnes says it is preparatory to summing up an argument so stated that the conclusion is inevitable, and Wesley marks off two conclusions, one about the Gentiles and one about Israel.

What is said of the Gentiles is a paradox, and treated as one. Henry says they followed not after righteousness, not knowing their guilt and misery and therefore not solicitous for a remedy, so that in their conversion preventing grace was greatly magnified, God being found of those who sought him not, nothing in them disposing them for such favour beyond what free grace wrought. Ellicott adds that they had no special revelation and were inattentive to the law of conscience. Barnes guards it, since it does not mean none of them had any solicitude about right and wrong, but that they had not made it their pursuit as the Jew had. Robertson notes that the verb keeps up the figure of the chase, meaning to grasp or overtake, and calls it a curious paradox. Calvin says nothing appeared more unreasonable than that men with no concern for righteousness, who rolled themselves in the lasciviousness of the flesh, should be called to salvation.

Of Israel the reverse is said outright. Gill observes that they were zealous of the law, called the law of righteousness because the matter of it was righteous, and that they tugged and toiled with all their might, as men running a race, to come up to it. Barnes explains that the just law demands perfect purity, and that they supposed their obedience a meritorious ground of justification. Clarke says they were industrious in observing a rule by which they thought to secure the blessings of God's kingdom, yet never came up to the true and only rule. Robertson says the verb means simply to arrive, and that legal righteousness they failed to reach because it required keeping the whole law perfectly. Ellicott says they tried to keep the law but failed to bring themselves under its protection, and notes that the second righteousness is absent from the best manuscripts. Calvin puts it that by running out of the way they wearied themselves in vain.

The reason given divides them. Gill says they sought righteousness neither in the right object, seeking it in the law where a sinful creature can never find it, nor in the right way, which is by faith. Barnes says they depended on their own righteousness and not on the mercy of God, and answers how they could have known better from the older Scriptures and the reference of the sacrifices. Clarke says that being ignorant of God's method they went about to establish their own, attending not to the covenant with Abraham, which stands on the extensive principles of grace and faith, but turning all their regard to the law. Calvin says false zeal commonly seems justly excused, but that they are deservedly rejected who attempt salvation by trusting their own works, since so far as in them lies they abolish faith, and their success would be the annihilation of true righteousness. Wesley asks what the others do not: was it because God eternally decreed they should not attain? and answers that there is nothing like this to be met with, the reason given being that they sought it not by faith.
33:
The citation is composite, and they take pains over it. Gill says the beginning and the end come from one passage and the middle from the other, an instance of the skipping from place to place about which the Jewish reading rules had something to say. Calvin traces the same seams and calls the citation remarkable in its manner, though the subject is one. Ellicott calls it a free combination and distinguishes the originals, since in the first the prophet refers to the temple's foundation stone as a symbol of divine faithfulness and in the second to God himself; the apostle, like the Jewish teachers, applied both to the Messiah, and not wrongly, for they foretold the triumph of the theocracy fulfilled in him. He adds that the two appear together elsewhere with a similar variation though kept distinct, and Robertson infers either that one apostle had read the other or that both had a collection of such testimonies.

Barnes traces the place name through its senses: the hill in Jerusalem over against the temple mount, where David's palace was and the court resided; then the whole city; then the capital and glory of the people of God; and hence the church itself, which is its meaning here. The word rock he derives from the custom of building, the same one being the corner stone on which the church is reared, not on human merits but by the righteousness of the Saviour; the stone designed as a corner stone became by their own wickedness the block over which they fell into ruin. He adds carefully that he is called a rock of stumbling not because it was the design of sending him that men should fall, but because such would be the result. Wesley says the same from the other side, that God exhibits in his church what, though in truth the only sure foundation of happiness, will in fact be a stumbling stone and an occasion of ruin through obstinate unbelief. Robertson renders the second phrase a rock of snare, a rock which they made a cause of stumbling.

Clarke explains why the offence was taken. The Messiah promised was a widely different person from the one they expected, for whereas they looked for a mighty secular prince to set up a secular kingdom, he appeared a man of sorrows acquainted with griefs, and redeemed mankind not by his sword but by his humiliation, passion and death; therefore they were offended and rejected him, thinking it reproachful to trust such a person for salvation.

The closing promise is read as consolation. Calvin says this part is subjoined for the comfort of the godly: because he is called the stone of stumbling there is no reason we should dread him or fear instead of trusting, since he is appointed for ruin to the unbelieving but for life and resurrection to the godly; the same one is a firm stone, precious, a corner stone most firmly fixed, and whoever builds on it shall never fall. Clarke says that so far shall any be from confusion or disappointment that every genuine believer shall find salvation, remission of sins here and eternal glory hereafter. On the last words the versions differ, and all of them notice it. Ellicott and Robertson record simply that the Hebrew reads shall not make haste. Barnes explains how the two meet, since the word also means to be afraid, as one who makes haste often is, and so comes near the sense of shame; the believer shall not be agitated by fear of failure nor disappointed of his hope. Calvin reaches the same result, that the Hebrew will bear the sense of hurrying or being confounded, and that since the Lord there bids us hope well it follows that we cannot be ashamed.
